doc.title: Larry Ridley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 10, 2003

title: Sixties sideman years: Newport All-Stars, Joe Venuti and the myth of New Orleans
summary: Asked about the sixties, he mentions his album Sum of the Parts, touring with the Newport All-Stars and Joe Venuti, and denies jazz was born only in New Orleans.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: Man. Let me return to your own career here for a minute. The sixties were quite an amazing era for you it seems. I don’t know if you can divide it into just the sixties, but you played with a long, long list. Does anybody stand out in your own mind, particular tours or recordings that you’d just like to mention?

All of it really. I mean it all is — each entity is one component or one part — when I say sum of the parts that’s the reason why like my first album that I produced is called “Sum” S-U-M “of the Parts.” Because I recognized that I’m the sum total of all these influences, all these people, everything that I’ve studied, everything that I’ve dedicated myself to in terms of my spirituality, my learning, my friendships with people and just trying to understand what the totality of life is all about. And it’s an ongoing quest. And traveling with the Newport Jazz Festival All-Stars, sitting in the lobby in Tokyo, Japan with Joe Venuti and talking about music and hanging out with this guy and hearing his ideas. I would ask him, I’d say, “Joe, where did jazz come from? Where did you hear jazz?” He’d say, “Oh it came from the black people and that’s how I learned it.” And when I was playing with Paul Whiteman’s group I took stuff back to him. Plus Paul Whiteman’s father you know was involved with teaching Lester Young.

Yeah. That’s — and you know you have the Pettiford family? All these territories. See and that’s another thing that I am very, very adamant about too is this mythology about jazz being born only in New Orleans is a myth. Absolute myth. And I did my homework with Eubie Blake and Garvin Bushell and Doc Cheatham and people like this. And they said wherever there was a significant population of people of African descent they were creating a spontaneous improvised hot music. That’s why you have the Afro-Cuban improvisation. That’s their way of playing, it’s essentially jazz. They’re improvising, right? So and if we look at the different parts of the United States they were playing music. I mean people in Chicago weren’t waiting on King Oliver to get off the riverboat and say come on in here King Oliver and teach us how to play jazz. They were already playing jazz. What was James Reese Europe doing in New York? The blues wasn’t just born in the Mississippi Delta. Excuse me? Hello? If you believe in that I mean you need to get AT&T long distance or something or Worldcom. No not Worldcom, that’s right, they failed. Anyway you know what I mean. But all of the people that I played with during the sixties had a profound influence on me. Sonny Rollins, John Coltrane, Dizzy Gillespie, Duke Ellington. All these people that you see listed that I have made sure that I listed at my web site and that I’m continuously reminded of, making sure I include all the people. Even people that a lot of people are not even aware of or may never have heard of or may never even understand their significance. They were significant to me because I learned from them. And I learned early on how to talk with people and not at or to.
